title: What smart people are saying about Trump's ban on new Chinese humanoid robots
byline: Aditi Bharade, Shubhangi Goel, Tom Carter
excerpt: Government authorities deemed that the robots pose "unacceptable safety risks" to national security.

The Trump Administration's crackdown on Chinese robots is getting mixed reactions.

On Tuesday, the Federal Communications Commission announced the administration's ban on new imports of "advanced robotic devices" from China, including humanoid and quadrupeds. The ban also extends to China-made power inverters used in batteries and data centers.

The FCC said the ban was imposed because these robots "pose unacceptable safety risks to the national security of the United States."

Robots that have already been brought to the US before the ban was announced will not be affected by it.

Here's what smart people in policy, tech, and venture capital are saying about the ban.

Chris McGuire, senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations

Responding to FCC Chair Brendan Carr's X post about the ban, Chris McGuire said this was a "very, very big deal."

McGuire is a senior fellow for China and emerging technology at the Council on Foreign Relations.

He said in his Tuesday X post that the ban will incentivize the US to shore up its robotics supply chains while "preventing China from flooding the US market with cheap robots that also pose national security risks (similar to Chinese connected vehicles)."

McGuire praised the tactic of imposing import bans on specific rapidly growing technologies from China that could pose national security risks to the US.

Rush Doshi, director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations

Rush Doshi, the director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations, called the ban "one of the most significant actions taken so far in support of the U.S. robotics ecosystem."

Reposting Carr's X post, Doshi compared the move to the FCC's announcement last December regarding restrictions on new foreign-made drones.

"The FCC's drone action was a shot in the arm for the domestic drone industry, and I think this has that same potential in robotics," Doshi wrote.

Doshi was the deputy senior director for China and Taiwan on the National Security Council under former President Joe Biden.

Peter Harrell, visiting scholar at Georgetown Law School

Peter Harrell, a visiting scholar at Georgetown's Institute of International Economic Law, called the ban an "important national security move," adding that advanced robots collect vast amounts of data and are integrated into key industries.

"This should provide a substantial tailwind to U.S. and allied inverter and robot manufacturers," Harrell wrote on X. He said the move will protect the US market and create space for its companies to expand.

Ramez Naam, founder of Planetary VC

In an X post on Tuesday, climate investor Ramez Naam described the new ban as a "double-edged sword."

"Short term, the rest of the world will have access to better cheaper hum/quad robots than the US," he wrote. "Longer term, with luck, US industry will thrive. But China will have advantage of a larger market indefinitely."

He said that humanoid robots are a "terrible form factor" for warfare and are unlikely to affect defense. But the ban on quadrupeds, animal-like robots that walk on four legs, could have consequences for defense.

Justin Lopas, founder of Base Power

Justin Lopas, the founder of home battery system provider Base Power, gave a nod of support to the ban.

"For those in the know, this is a very big deal," Lopas wrote on X.

The founder worked in manufacturing and mechanical engineering at SpaceX and Anduril before launching his company in 2023.

David Hansen, cofounder of Westmag

David Hansen, the cofounder and CEO of Westmag, a US manufacturer of drone motors and robot actuators backed by Andreessen Horowitz, wrote in a post on X that China's robotics industry will shrug off the ban.

"Their entire annual export business, to every country on earth, is what they moved at home in four weeks. We are a rounding error to them," he wrote.

Hansen added that unless the US builds up its own robotics supply chain, it risks falling well behind China's booming robotics industry as adoption increases.

"At some point soon, millions of Americans will open Tiktok and watch Chinese robots cooking dinner, folding laundry, and cleaning the homes of ordinary people in Shenzhen. Demand will flip overnight, every American will suddenly want one," Hansen added.

Ted Xiao, founding member of technical staff at Prometheus

Ted Xiao, a founding member of technical staff at Jeff Bezos' Prometheus AI startup, wrote on X that the ban would herald a wave of pain for US robotics startups.

"Every single live player in robotics + AI relies on Chinese hardware; the US robotics hardware ecosystem is years behind," the former Google DeepMind scientist said.

Chris Paxton, innovation lead at Agility

Chris Paxton, an AI innovation lead at robotics company Agility — which is planning to go public at a $2.5 billion valuation — wrote on X that the ban would harm US developers who use affordable Chinese robots as development and testing units for robotics and AI software.

"So lets say I want to start a humanoid company, making brains/software (American competitive advantage). What exactly are my options in the USA, now?" wrote the former Meta and Nvidia researcher.

Deedy Das, partner at Menlo Ventures

In an episode of the "This Week in Startups" podcast released on Wednesday, Das said the US should subject robotics to far more scrutiny than it does AI models.

"The kind of damage vectors on language models are far more restrictive than what can happen with robotics," he said.

The VC added that it is quite difficult for the US to manufacture robots at the prices Chinese companies are offering.

"They are astounding that they can get this low. America needs to do something to be able to compete in the same way that it had to for the chips and LLM landscape," he said.

Jason Calacanis, tech podcaster and angel investor

On the same podcast released on Wednesday, Calacanis called the ban "smart."

"You wouldn't want to have a situation where one morning 10,000 of these woke up with the instructions to take out a terrorist attack," he said, referring to humanoid robots. "I know it sounds fantastical, but if I told you, 50 years ago, that terrorists would take two airplanes and crash them into the World Trade Center, you'd be like, 'that's insane.'"

作者：Aditi Bharade 您目前正在关注该作者！ 想要取消关注吗？ 通过电子邮件中的链接取消订阅。 , Shubhangi Goel 您目前正在关注该作者！ 想要取消关注吗？ 通过电子邮件中的链接取消订阅。和汤姆·卡特 您目前正在关注该作者！ 想要取消关注吗？ 通过电子邮件中的链接取消订阅。

特朗普政府对中国机器人的打压引起了不同的反应。

周二，美国联邦通信委员会宣布政府禁止从中国进口新的“先进机器人设备”，包括人形机器人和四足动物。 该禁令还适用于电池和数据中心使用的中国制造的逆变器。

美国联邦通信委员会表示，实施禁令是因为这些机器人“对美国国家安全构成了不可接受的安全风险”。

在禁令宣布之前已经进入美国的机器人将不会受到该禁令的影响。

以下是政策、技术和风险投资领域的聪明人对这项禁令的看法。

克里斯·麦奎尔，外交关系委员会高级研究员

克里斯·麦奎尔 (Chris McGuire) 在回应 FCC 主席布伦丹·卡尔 (Brendan Carr) 关于该禁令的 X 帖子时表示，这是一件“非常非常大的事情”。

麦奎尔是外交关系委员会中国和新兴技术高级研究员。

他在周二的帖子中表示，该禁令将激励美国加强其机器人供应链，同时“防止中国用廉价机器人涌入美国市场，这些机器人也构成国家安全风险（类似于中国的联网汽车）。”

麦奎尔赞扬了对来自中国的特定快速增长技术实施进口禁令的策略，这些技术可能对美国构成国家安全风险。

拉什·多西（Rush Doshi），外交关系委员会中国战略倡议主任

美国外交关系委员会中国战略倡议主任拉什·多西（Rush Doshi）称该禁令是“迄今为止为支持美国机器人生态系统而采取的最重要行动之一”。

多西转发了卡尔的 X 帖子，将此举与 FCC 去年 12 月关于限制新型外国制造无人机的声明进行了比较。

多西写道：“美国联邦通信委员会的无人机行动为国内无人机行业注入了一剂强心剂，我认为这在机器人技术领域也具有同样的潜力。”

多西是前总统乔·拜登领导下的国家安全委员会中国和台湾事务副高级主任。

Peter Harrell，乔治城法学院访问学者

乔治城国际经济法研究所访问学者彼得·哈勒尔称该禁令是“重要的国家安全举措”，并补充说先进的机器人收集大量数据并融入关键行业。

哈勒尔在 X 上写道：“这将为美国及其盟国逆变器和机器人制造商提供巨大的推动力。” 他表示，此举将保护美国市场，并为其企业扩张创造空间。

Ramez Naam，Planetary VC 创始人

气候投资者 Ramez Naam 在周二的 X 帖子中将新禁令描述为一把“双刃剑”。

“短期内，世界其他地区将能够获得比美国更好、更便宜的嗡嗡声/四轮机器人，”他写道。 “从长远来看，如果幸运的话，美国工业将会蓬勃发展。 但中国将无限期地拥有更大市场的优势。”

他说，人形机器人对于战争来说是一种“可怕的外形因素”，不太可能影响防御。 但对四足动物（四足行走的类似动物的机器人）的禁令可能会对国防产生影响。

贾斯汀·洛帕斯（Justin Lopas），Base Power 创始人

家用电池系统提供商 Base Power 的创始人贾斯汀·洛帕斯 (Justin Lopas) 对该禁令表示支持。

洛帕斯在 X 上写道：“对于知情人士来说，这是一件大事。”

在 2023 年创办公司之前，创始人曾在 SpaceX 和 Anduril 从事制造和机械工程工作。

大卫·汉森，Westmag 联合创始人

由Andreessen Horowitz支持的美国无人机电机和机器人执行器制造商Westmag的联合创始人兼首席执行官大卫·汉森(David Hansen)在X上发帖称，中国的机器人行业将摆脱禁令。

“他们向地球上每个国家的全部年度出口业务，都是他们在四个星期内搬回国内的。 我们对他们来说是一个四舍五入的错误，”他写道。

汉森补充说，除非美国建立自己的机器人供应链，否则随着采用率的增加，美国可能会远远落后于中国蓬勃发展的机器人行业。

“很快的某个时候，数百万美国人将打开抖音，观看中国机器人做饭、叠衣服、打扫深圳老百姓的家。 需求将在一夜之间发生转变，每个美国人都会突然想要一个，”汉森补充道。

Ted Shaw，Prometheus 创始技术人员

杰夫·贝索斯 (Jeff Bezos) 的普罗米修斯人工智能初创公司的技术人员创始成员特德·肖 (Ted Shaw) 在 X 上写道，这项禁令将预示着美国机器人初创公司将迎来一波痛苦。

这位前谷歌 DeepMind 科学家表示：“机器人+人工智能领域的每一个参与者都依赖中国硬件；美国的机器人硬件生态系统落后了很多年。”

Chris Paxton，Agility 创新主管

机器人公司 Agility 的人工智能创新主管 Chris Paxton（该公司计划以 25 亿美元的估值上市）在 X 上写道，这项禁令将损害美国开发商的利益，因为他们使用负担得起的中国机器人作为机器人和人工智能软件的开发和测试单位。

“假设我想创办一家人形公司，制造大脑/软件（美国的竞争优势）。 现在我在美国到底有什么选择？” 前 Meta 和 Nvidia 研究员写道。

Deedy Das，Menlo Ventures 合伙人

在周三发布的“本周初创公司”播客的一集中，达斯表示，美国应该对机器人技术进行比对人工智能模型更严格的审查。

“语言模型上的损伤向量比机器人技术上可能发生的损伤向量要严格得多，”他说。

该风险投资公司补充说，美国很难以中国公司提供的价格制造机器人。

“他们令人惊讶的是他们能降到如此低的水平。 美国需要采取一些措施，才能像在芯片和法学硕士领域那样进行竞争，”他说。

Jason Calacanis，科技播客兼天使投资人

在周三发布的同一个播客中，卡拉卡尼斯称这项禁令是“明智的”。

他说：“你不会希望出现这样一种情况：一天早上，一万名机器人醒来时收到了消灭恐怖袭击的指示。”他指的是人形机器人。 “我知道这听起来很荒诞，但如果我在 50 年前告诉你，恐怖分子会驾驶两架飞机撞向世贸中心，你会说，‘这太疯狂了。’”
